title: Towards Understanding Modality Interaction in Multimodal Language Models via Partial Information Decomposition
claim: A conditional information-theoretic decomposition pipeline can diagnose how a multimodal model combines its input modalities into one decision.
layout: Single wide panel, left-to-right flow, nested shaded sub-boxes feeding a vertical estimator bar
description: A wide left-to-right pipeline diagram. On the left, a pink box shows video and audio input and a yellow box shows an example multiple-choice prompt about which instrument is playing. Both feed a tall teal box labeled omni-modal models, with a thought-bubble question beneath. Next is a teal 'Shared Multimodal Token Space' panel. It shows vision tokens (teal) and audio tokens (pink) being mean-pooled into features X and Y, with masked variants. Below it, a yellow 'Text-Conditioned Predictive Distributions' panel shows forward passes through the model and the resulting answer probabilities for audio-only, vision-only and joint inputs. A tall pink vertical bar labeled BATCH Estimator follows. A big arrow then leads to a bar chart of U_vis, U_aud, R_sens and S_av. Beside the chart, a gray box lists analyses: interaction regime, modality bias and layer-wise dynamics. Teal stands for vision and pink for audio throughout.
caption: The Sensory PID Framework. (Left) Omni-modal models are analyzed by treating the text prompt as a conditioning signal for video–audio interaction. (Right) Applying the BATCH estimator in the shared token space decomposes decision-level information into Unique (Uvis, Uaud), Redundant (Rsens), and Synergistic (Sav) components.
abstract: Understanding how multimodal large language models use different modalities is important for reliable reasoning. We employ Partial Information Decomposition (PID) as a decision-level lens and introduce Sensory PID, a conditional formulation that conditions on language and separates unique, redundant, and synergistic contributions from video and audio. Applied to omni-modal models, Sensory PID reveals a sensory synergy bottleneck: even on audio-visual fusion tasks, decisions remain dominated by modality-unique information, with stronger reliance on vision. Modality-shuffling interventions support this asymmetry, while layer-wise analysis reveals a visual-first computation pattern and instruction perturbations show that late-stage sensory fusion is conditioned by language. Beyond diagnosis, PID-guided sample reweighting provides initial evidence that local diagnostic signals can improve multimodal reasoning and grounding performance. As reference validation, our vision-language analysis broadly corroborates previously reported decision-level PID patterns across tasks, models, interventions, and layers.
